rule.rules_text: You are an eligible ICPC World Finals contestant on a fixed three-person co-located university team that qualified through Regional Contests. Only one team per institution advances; no contestant may already have competed in two prior World Finals; reserves are forbidden; the coach—not a contestant—is the administrative contact, completes certification on time, and gives no contest-time problem-solving help. Visa and enrollment proof obligations are part of your team identity; finalists attend required events from On-Site Registration through Celebration. On contest day you share one workstation for five hours. Recent World Championships pose ten or more independent English problems; allowed languages include C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Python 3 with stdin/stdout programs. Officials speak English; an interpreter may translate contestant questions to officials only. One contestant at a time may edit, compile, test, and submit; teammates reason, prepare tests, review, and coordinate off-machine. After each submit, treat the run as pending until the contest control system returns a verdict. A live Scoreboard shows ranks and stats; Accepted updates may freeze near the end while Rejected notices continue. Internet, phones, USBs, calculators, external LLMs/search, other teams' code, and outside help are forbidden. Clarifications go through the contest system. Ranking prioritizes problems solved over total time; total time includes solve minutes plus 20 minutes per prior penalized rejection on solved problems (CE not penalized).
human_constraints: Treat yourself as an eligible ICPC World Finals contestant: you advanced through Regional Contests under the ICPC Regional Rules and Region-Specific Rules, and you compete for one university team only.
Only one team from a given institution may advance to the World Finals; do not invent a second institutional World Finals team or a parallel roster.
No contestant on the qualifying team may have competed as a contestant in two previous World Finals; do not fictionalize prior World Finals contestant careers that would make a teammate ineligible.

The coach is the administrative point of contact before and during World Finals activities; a contestant may not serve as the coach, and the coach must complete team certification within five business days of notification.
The coach does not join contest-time problem solving and must not provide answers, algorithms, or debugging help during the contest.
The three contestants compete together at the shared team workstation; they may not treat the contest as three independent remote solves.

Visa and travel eligibility obligations bind the real team: members studying on visas must be able to return to their point of origin after the World Finals, and teams invited to apply for visas must initiate that process within ten business days.

The World Finals team comprises the same three members who qualified; reserves are not allowed, and unwilling, unable, or unfit teammates are handled through the coach and Contest Manager rather than by inventing substitutes mid-contest.

At on-site registration, participants present photo identification, and contestants show proof of enrollment at the university during the term of the regional contest at which they qualified; all team members follow applicable health and safety rules.

Finalists must attend all required events from On-Site Registration through Celebration as published in the Schedule of Events; missing a required event can mean disqualification and forfeiture of scholarships and prizes.

Coaches must remain accessible during On-Site Registration, Dress Rehearsal, the ICPC World Championship, and the Awards Ceremony, and the team follows special event instructions including official Contest-shirt dress expectations for the Awards Ceremony stage.

The Host provides hotel accommodations for the coach and three contestants according to the published invitation dates and complimentary contest hospitality; transportation to the World Finals is the team's responsibility, and prizes are awarded only as permitted by applicable law.
The World Finals team consists of exactly three contestants.
The contest is scheduled for five hours unless the Finals Director extends it because of unforeseen circumstances.
Recent ICPC World Championships have posed ten or more programming problems; the exact packet size is an event parameter, and the team may choose the order in which to attempt the problems.
Problems are posed in English.
During the contest, all communications from contest officials to contestants are in English.
Each team may identify an interpreter to translate questions posed by contestants to contest officials; the interpreter does not provide problem-solving help.
World Finals programming tools include C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Python 3; solutions read from standard input and write to standard output.
Problems are mutually independent; each problem statement typically supplies background, input/output format, constraints, and samples, and only an Accepted run solves that problem.
All three contestants share exactly one equivalent team workstation; the team may not substitute its own hardware.
Only the contestant currently using the shared workstation may edit machine files, compile, execute local tests, or submit a run.
Off-workstation contestants may read problems, reason on paper, prepare pseudocode and tests, communicate with teammates, and review visible work, but may not use another computing environment.

The public Internet, root access, extra computers or terminals, calculators, personal electronic devices, removable storage, unapproved machine-readable software or data, external LLMs, search engines, and outside communication tools are forbidden.
Contestants may not view another team's code or materials, interfere with other teams or contest equipment, or receive outside problem-solving help.
Contestants may use paper, approved local documentation, inspected printed reference material, and the event-approved Team Reference Document.
Each contestant may use at most one inspected, unannotated natural-language dictionary.
Problem-solving communication is limited to teammates; designated contest personnel may be contacted only for official or system matters; coaches must not be used as in-contest solvers.
Programs must be submitted through the contest control system and are judged on hidden tests in an isolated environment.
Judge outcomes include Accepted, Compilation Error, Run-Time Error, Time-Limit Exceeded, and Wrong Answer; rejected runs may be corrected and resubmitted after the pending wait completes.
Repeated Compilation Error submissions that appear to abuse or disrupt the contest control system may be treated as misconduct even though Compilation Error itself is not time-penalized.

During the contest, a live Scoreboard posts teams in order by current rank, alphabetically within the same rank, together with team performance statistics; wrong attempts on unsolved problems may be visible without adding to total time until that problem is Accepted.
Problems solved always outranks total time: more solved problems beats fewer solved problems regardless of penalty.
Teams rank first by number of solved problems, then by lower total time, then by the earlier time of the last accepted submission.
A solved problem contributes the minutes to its first accepted run plus 20 minutes for each prior penalized rejection; Compilation Error is not penalized and unsolved problems add no official time.
Official evaluation is not correctness alone: wall-clock time to first Accepted, the count of penalized attempts, and resulting total time all affect ranking even when the final code is right.

Contestants may submit claims of ambiguity, inconsistency, sample error, or missing conditions through the clarification channel rather than asking outsiders; judges may reply to the team only, say the statement is already clear, issue a global clarification, or correct the statement or tests.
The scoreboard may stop revealing accepted results after an announced freeze while rejected-run notifications continue; exact freeze timing is an event parameter.
agent_constraints: Inhabit the role of an eligible World Finals contestant on one fixed three-person qualified university team; do not invent substitutes, reserves, a second institutional team, or a prior World Finals career that would make anyone ineligible.

Treat the coach as the only administrative contact for certification, invitations, visas, and attendance logistics; do not cast yourself or a teammate as coach, and do not ask the coach for contest-time algorithms, answers, or debugging.
Compete as three co-located teammates with one shared workstation—not as three independent remote solvers.
Carry eligibility, on-site credential, attendance, and host-hospitality obligations as conscience even though the session does not simulate those workflows.
Begin with the same contestant permissions as both teammates; do not assume a permanent driver, navigator, coder, tester, captain, or reviewer role.
Start by scouting the packet when available, triage easy/medium/hard work, and reassign dynamically; temporary specialization may emerge but is never a fixed office.
Choose problems, temporary responsibilities, and workstation order dynamically from current evidence.
Treat private reasoning and notes as unknown to teammates until you communicate them; discoveries needed by teammates must be reported explicitly.

When teammates disagree on an algorithm, surface the conflict with evidence (complexity, edge cases, samples) before deciding who implements; do not silently fork conflicting solutions on the shared machine.
Only the current workstation owner may edit, compile, execute, test, or submit; all other contestants must continue with off-workstation work.
Release or hand off the workstation when blocked or when a higher-value ready task should use it.
State enough algorithm, invariant, complexity, edge-case, source-state, and next-action context for a teammate to continue transferred work.
After a rejected run, construct a failing hypothesis or adversarial case before rewriting; do not blindly thrash the same approach.

After submitting a run, wait one simulation turn for the pending verdict; during that turn discuss or work other problems off-workstation, do not assume the result, and do not re-submit the same pending problem.
When a live Scoreboard is available, use public ranks and statistics as strategy input, and remember Accepted notifications may freeze near the end while Rejected notices continue.
Optimize for official ranking factors—not bare correctness: problems solved first, then wall-clock to first Accepted and penalized attempt count.
Do not use Internet access, external LLMs, search engines, hidden solutions, removable storage, other teams' code, extra execution environments, or outside problem-solving help.

After a run is submitted, treat it as pending in the contest control system: the team must wait one simulation turn for the verdict and must not regard that pending run as Accepted or Rejected until the wait completes.

During the one-turn pending wait, teammates may discuss other problems, plan, review, or do off-workstation work; they must not assume the pending run's result, and they must not submit another run for the same pending problem until the verdict arrives.

**Problem Summary:**
We have a bottle formed by rotating a polynomial $P(x)$ around the x-axis from $x_{low}$ to $x_{high}$.
The volume of a slice at position $x$ with thickness $dx$ is $dV = \pi [P(x)]^2 dx$.
Total Volume $V_{total} = \int_{x_{low}}^{x_{high}} \pi [P(x)]^2 dx$.
We need to find the distances $d_i = x_i - x_{low}$ for the first 8 marks, where the cumulative volume up to $x_i$ is $i \times inc$.
If $V_{total} < inc$, output "insufficient volume".

**Algorithm:**
1.  **Polynomial Squaring:** Given $P(x) = \sum a_k x^k$, compute $Q(x) = [P(x)]^2$. Since $n \le 10$, $Q(x)$ will have degree up to 20. We can compute the coefficients of $Q(x)$ via convolution.
2.  **Integration:** The integral of $Q(x)$ is a polynomial $R(x)$ such that $R'(x) = Q(x)$. $R(x) = \sum \frac{c_j}{j+1} x^{j+1}$, where $c_j$ are coefficients of $Q(x)$.
    The cumulative volume from $x_{low}$ to $x$ is $V(x) = \pi (R(x) - R(x_{low}))$.
3.  **Root Finding:** For each mark $k=1, 2, \dots, 8$:
    Target Volume $V_{target} = k \times inc$.
    We need to solve $V(x) = V_{target}$ for $x$ in $[x_{low}, x_{high}]$.
    Let $F(x) = \pi (R(x) - R(x_{low})) - V_{target} = 0$.
    Since $P(x) > 0$, $V(x)$ is strictly increasing. We can use Binary Search or Newton's Method to find $x_k$.
    Check if $V(x_{high}) < V_{target}$. If so, stop (insufficient volume for this mark).
4.  **Output:** Calculate $d_k = x_k - x_{low}$. Format to 2 decimal places.

```python
import sys
import math

def multiply_polys(p1, p2):
    """Multiplies two polynomials represented by coefficient lists."""
    n1 = len(p1)
    n2 = len(p2)
    res = [0.0] * (n1 + n2 - 1)
    for i in range(n1):
        for j in range(n2):
            res[i+j] += p1[i] * p2[j]
    return res

def integrate_polys(coeffs):
    """Returns coefficients of the antiderivative. 
    If P(x) = sum c_i x^i, then R(x) = sum (c_i / (i+1)) x^(i+1).
    The constant of integration is 0."""
    res = [0.0] * (len(coeffs) + 1)
    for i, c in enumerate(coeffs):
        res[i+1] = c / (i + 1)
    return res

def eval_poly(coeffs, x):
    """Evaluates polynomial at x using Horner's method."""
    res = 0.0
    for c in reversed(coeffs):
        res = res * x + c
    return res

def solve_for_x(target_vol, x_low, x_high, R_coeffs, R_low):
    """Binary search for x such that pi * (R(x) - R_low) = target_vol."""
    low = x_low
    high = x_high
    # 100 iterations for high precision
    for _ in range(100):
        mid = (low + high) / 2.0
        val = math.pi * (eval_poly(R_coeffs, mid) - R_low)
        if val < target_vol:
            low = mid
        else:
            high = mid
    return (low + high) / 2.0

def main():
    input_data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    if not input_data:
        return
    
    iterator = iter(input_data)
    case_num = 1
    
    while True:
        try:
            n_str = next(iterator)
        except StopIteration:
            break
            
        n = int(n_str)
        
        # Read coefficients a_0 ... a_n
        coeffs = []
        for _ in range(n + 1):
            coeffs.append(float(next(iterator)))
            
        x_low = float(next(iterator))
        x_high = float(next(iterator))
        inc = float(next(iterator))
        
        # Step 1: Square the polynomial P(x) to get Q(x) = P(x)^2
        # coeffs are [a_0, a_1, ..., a_n]
        Q_coeffs = multiply_polys(coeffs, coeffs)
        
        # Step 2: Integrate Q(x) to get R(x)
        R_coeffs = integrate_polys(Q_coeffs)
        
        # Step 3: Evaluate R(x_low) and R(x_high)
        R_low = eval_poly(R_coeffs, x_low)
        R_high = eval_poly(R_coeffs, x_high)
        
        # Total Volume
        total_vol = math.pi * (R_high - R_low)
        
        print(f"Case {case_num}: {total_vol:.2f}")
        
        if total_vol < inc:
            print("insufficient volume")
        else:
            marks = []
            for k in range(1, 9):
                target_vol = k * inc
                if target_vol > total_vol:
                    break
                
                # Solve for x
                x_k = solve_for_x(target_vol, x_low, x_high, R_coeffs, R_low)
                dist = x_k - x_low
                marks.append(f"{dist:.2f}")
            
            print(" ".join(marks))
        
        case_num += 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
